<reason>PRO (B) built the clearer decision frame and exploited two real concessions: CON's "screen not crib, purge extras" line was persuasively recast as purpose restriction and short retention, and CON's own "notice plus office option" was shown to be structurally close to opt-in with a genuine alternative. CON fought back well—its A1 distinction (decline-and-commute vs. refuse-and-stay-home) was a legitimate answer PRO had wrongly pre-declared unanswered, and its A2 correctly identified that "no biometric inference" and mandatory human review do bite on identity matching. But PRO turned that A2 answer into its best moment: once CON admitted the presence check needs face-matching, long retention, and auto-firing flags, PRO's "not a floor walk, a face-recognition camera in a bedroom" reframe landed hard, and PRO's teller/copywriter model kept a live, coherent version of the motion that preserved security while blocking silent deployment. CON's "firms won't litigate seat by seat" fallback was speculative and met by the risk-based-access point. PRO carried execution costs (clipped opening, bogus [C1.5]/[C2.5] refs, premature "you named none"/"silence decides" claims), and CON's terse style hurt accessibility, so the result is a clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing seizing on CON's [A4.3] admission that the "modest" presence check actually requires biometric matching of home video, retained for later payroll disputes, with flags firing before any human looks—converting CON's answer to the pressure question into confirmation of PRO's intrusiveness thesis.</best_rebuttal>
